# Preface {#sec-preface .unnumbered}

You, the reader, likely fall into one of three groups: college students, students bound for college, or college instructors. A goal often claimed by colleges is that, among other things, they foster the development of critical thinking skills. While often used merely as a marketing slogan or mission statement, many college faculty press for the explicit teaching of critical thinking. This book is allied with that goal.

This book deals with critical thinking with quantitative information. Educators have identified four broad themes used for teaching critical thinking. Among these are 1) finding, evaluating, and using information effectively, 2) translating data and knowledge into formats that highlight key relationships, 3) building sound arguments based on evidence and knowledge, and 4) being aware of your own thinking patterns, including the development of new patterns and finding the appropriate level of skepticism toward your own and others’ conclusions.

An argument can be made that traditional mathematics education serves these themes, but I think it is a weak argument. When it comes to (1), statistics is a much better fit than algebra. And while algebra does provide a format for knowledge as in (2), it is very limited, leaving no room for uncertainty or even data. The mathematical approach to building sound arguments is centered on proof and symbolic manipulation. Unfortunately, it is hard to sufficiently pin down natural settings, even slightly complex ones, to render them susceptible to proof. Building sound arguments in practice often requires reasoning with incomplete information, uncertainty, and incomplete understanding.

The traditional approach is strongest in providing mechanisms for new patterns of thinking, for instance, the idea of marginal or instantaneous change, which has many applications in describing and analyzing the world around us. But the structure of the traditional curriculum puts the mathematical thinking patterns most central to using information out of reach for most students.

This book seeks to provide access to the quantitative concepts and skills that can support critical thinking. A central theme is modeling, the process of building quantitative representations of real-world systems. We make use of a concrete framework for modeling that can be taught and learned. In this framework, the system components are quantities. Conceptually, quantities are akin to numbers but include additional information that provides basic facts about how different kinds of quantities relate to one another.  The book uses almost no equations. Instead, the relationships between quantities in models are represented with functions and spaces. Equally important are the ideas of rates and rates of change.

These modeling tools are also elements of an important language for describing uncertainty and risk quantitatively. Increasingly, particularly over the last 40 years with the mainstream adoption of Bayesian inference, this language provides the means to use new observations and evidence to update our existing models.

Naturally, the point is not to build models for their own sake. They are built to allow us to extract information and conclusions that can inform our understanding of the real world and decision-making. Models also foster communication between individuals and groups, allowing us to resolve, through principled argument, the uncertainties and disagreements that often paralyze or divide us.

## Comments to instructors {.unnumbered}

The instructor interested in using this book or drawing from it to design a course is entitled to know why I have broken with many established conventions for teaching mathematics. My motivation has been skepticism: Are these conventions useful? What alternatives may be more effective for demonstrating that the mathematical topics are useful and provide new ways to think about important issues outside of mathematics?

Consider, for instance, the central role of algebra in the established curriculum. Mathematics instructors have generally been educated in the established curriculum and have come to think of algebra as an essential component of advanced mathematical thinking. We treat algebra as a way of explaining and a framework for student evaluation. We often define student success in terms of algebraic manipulation skills and whether the student is ready to take a calculus course. Some students, particularly the students we encounter in our university-level mathematics courses, have gained enough proficiency in algebraic manipulation to encourage us to use these skills as the foundation for further mathematical learning.

From the student point of view, however, the situation is different. A large fraction of students do not establish sufficient algebra skills to participate successfully in the university-level curriculum. Studies from professional organizations such as the Mathematical Association of America suggest that "a large fraction" means something like 80-90%. (To satisfy yourself that this is accurate, prompt an AI with this: "What fraction of college-bound students succeed in mastering algebra to an extent that they can use it effectively in university-level mathematics such as calculus?")

We temper our disappointment with this lack of success with assertions like, "Calculus is hard!" and "Not everyone is cut out for mathematics." And we make the most of our limited successes by accepting the contention that passing Calc I constitutes success. 

Before accepting this state of affairs, it is worth questioning whether another approach to presenting mathematical concepts could lead to greater understanding of the quantitative concepts used throughout our economy, society, and science. My experience over 30 years of college teaching is that de-emphasizing algebraic manipulation can enable students to access not just anecdotes of mathematical analysis but the very topics that appear in the third and later semesters of the traditional calculus curriculum: functions of multiple variables, partial derivatives (and their uses), linear algebra, and differential equations.

Naturally, I am not suggesting that students following an alternative pathway can do the problem sets associated with linear algebra or differential equations. But they can understand how dynamics are described and trajectories calculated. They can create an accurate mental picture of what it means to "train" a model or to evaluate trade-offs in realistic scenarios.

What are the alternatives to algebra-focused instruction? We can start by noting that most topics taught in a high-school algebra course are not relevant to the skills needed for quantitative analysis of systems and data. Factoring polynomials? Solving quadratic equations? Division of polynomials? You won't find them in this book. Better to build on foundational skills like understanding functions as transformations of inputs into outputs, and the graphical interpretation of relationships described by functions. 

Some, but not much, algebra is needed to understand rates of change, and an entirely adequate understanding can be developed from function graphics without formulas. Some, but not much, algebra is needed to work with dimensional analysis. The algebra of logarithms and $e^t$ need not interfere with developing an understanding of magnitudes and the ever-increasing rate of change in exponential growth. Emphasizing functional notation rather than the idiosyncrasies of $x^{-2}$, $\sqrt{3}{t}$, or $\sin^{-1}(x)$ removes many pitfalls and connects better to the computational environments (even in spreadsheets) that students will encounter in their careers. 

Famously, word problems are not a strong motivator of interest in algebra. It is better to set the goal as building representations of real-world systems and using these representations to extract meaningful insights and make informed decisions.

A good approximation to the conventional curriculum is "teaching algebra to reach calculus." The standard, and often encountered, alternative is, "teaching algebra for its own sake." Instead, this book emphasizes the kinds of relationships calculus was invented to describe, and how understanding those relationships guides decision-making and action. One such fundamental relationship is "rate of change." The book introduces it early (chapter 4) using only elementary algebra. The topic is used repeatedly in various contexts before introducing the nomenclature of derivatives and accumulation: describing functions, dimensional analysis, handling trade-offs, dealing with data and hypotheses using likelihood, and modeling dynamic systems.

Overall, the book's style *uses* mathematical concepts first, and minimize or even exclude the bathwater of mathematical formalisms such as limits. The flow of topics emphasizes mathematical description rather than the precise definition of ideas in mathematical terms. Students working through the book will develop an intuitive, practical understanding of the concepts and learn that, with further work, they can use them in their own work and applications. Students who have succeeded in the conventional mathematics curriculum generally gain a greatly enriched understanding of the mechanisms and applied purpose of the mathematical tools they have previously learned.

## Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

Although we often speak of writing a book as a journey, and a journey as a path followed, for this book the apt metaphor is "bushwhacking." At many points in my career, my view has been pulled left or right by a particular person or opportunity. A notable early influence was Leon Glass, my post-doc research advisor who used tools of mathematics to illuminate biology and physiology. Co-teaching with Leon in McGill's Biology 309 showed me how to motivate students with a simple trick: emphasizing quantitative topics that provide fresh, powerful insights into their primary interests. David Bressoud, then chair of the math/CS department at Macalester College, was willing to take a bet that hiring an engineer/physiologist/economist might enliven a stale math curriculum. Profs Stan Wagon and Wayne Roberts were active co-conspirators with David. Even before my job interview, Stan's well-known work using computing to open a window to understanding gave me confidence that my strengths in computing could make up for my severe weakness in theoretical mathematics.

My first years' observations at Macalester shocked me. Why were excellent teachers dwelling on antique topics? David, perhaps sensing my confusion, recruited me to participate in the late-1990s Curriculum Foundations project of the Math Association of America (led by William Barker and Susan Ganter). With equal numbers of math professors and faculty from a score of non-math fields (science, economics, business, etc.), the meetings revealed that non-mathematicians from a wide variety of perspectives largely shared the same critique of, and remedies for, the early college-level math curriculum. To pick just one example: There was unanimous support for removing "graphing calculators" from the curriculum so students could develop computing skills they will use in their careers. Except for the mathematicians, not one of the Foundations participants saw graphing calculators as a positive. And so, thirty years later, calculators remain a staple of high-school math classes.

In the friendly and supportive environment provided by David and the late Jan Serie (biology), I could propose to the then largest of the science departments at Macalester to replace their required calculus and statistics credits with modeling- and computing-based integrated calculus/statistics courses that eventually, as Math 135 and Stat 155, gained the largest enrollment of any at the college. Profs. Tom Halverson and Karen Saxe took the risk of co-teaching these yet-to-be-developed courses in the first two years. Their experience reassured the department faculty that highly meaningful math and statistics could be taught without the baggage of the traditional curriculum. Later, Profs Dan Flath, Chad Topaz, and Andrew Beveridge lent their skill and enthusiasm to enhancing the courses, securing them as a stable entry point to the quantitative curriculum.

In the same period, David and I proposed an experimental demonstration that students from all fields, as well as their faculty mentors from fields skeptical about the relevance of math, would value mathematics that clearly illuminated social and economic policy debates, particularly year-long examinations of immigration policy and school vouchers. This became the Quantitative Methods for Public Policy graduation requirement, which has now, almost 20 years later, been reframed as a "Quantitative Argumentation" requirement for all students.

The innovations in teaching statistics that featured in Stat 155 were enthusiastically received by the statistics education community. The esteemed Prof. George Cobb (Mt. Holyoke) became a highly influential advocate, and Profs. Randall Pruim (Calvin College) and Nicholas Horton (Amherst College) helped to inspire and refine ideas. They developed an outstanding professional computing outreach program to help faculty gain the necessary skills. In this work, they joined me in organizing a 7-year National Science Foundation program that sought to integrate modeling, statistics, computation, and calculus---the MOSAIC topics---in the math curriculum. The statistics and data science textbooks that emerged from MOSAIC acknowledge the scores of faculty, across the US and internationally, who embraced the new capabilities for teaching authentically useful statistics at the earliest points in the college curriculum.

Mathematics education, however, remains deeply conservative. It largely ignored the Foundations project's recommendations even while accepting the improved pedagogy offered by the Calculus Reform movement. Despite wide recognition that the mathematics curriculum is the biggest obstacle to student participation in STEM fields, little changed. At least, until 2019, when the US Air Force Academy determined to rebuild, practically from scratch, their required core calculus courses, Math 141/142. Prof. Michael Brilleslyper, Prof. Bradley Warner, Colonel Scott Williams, and the Academy leadership invited me to work with them, with support from the Academy Research and Development Institute. Captains (now Majors) Ray Hill and Austin Davis provided energy, enthusiasm, and skill to develop and deploy the new core courses. Lt. Col. Kenneth Horton and Prof. Joseph Eichholz provided helpful suggestions and support; Ken shepharded the courses through the Academy's curriculum committee.

The USAFA calculus course drew on MOSAIC ideas, extending them into a full sequence that supports the technical needs of USAFA's engineering and science requirements. There, the story takes a surprising turn.

The University of Austin, established in 2024 by founders concerned about groupthink in academia, set out to inaugurate a true core curriculum. All students, as a major part of their college study, engage in the same topics simultaneously, as a shared experience. UATX broke with the near-universal practice of splitting students among many "entry points" to the traditional curriculum, from "college algebra" and "pre-calculus" onward. The spirit of a core curriculum called for all students to share the same entry point, despite marked variation in mathematical aptitude, enthusiasm, motivation, and eventual concentration. The core courses also had to be accessible and attractive, and enable all to work to success, regardless of their previous training.

UATX recruited Commander David Ruth from the US Naval Academy and commissioned him to oversee the core quantitative and STEM curriculum. David knew me from the MOSAIC project and the USAFA initiative. He invited me to join the UATX faculty. It was relatively easy to design one of the core courses around data, statistical modeling, causality, and risk. The other was initially framed around "quantitative literacy," which assembles an uncoordinated set of topics drawn from an elementary curriculum while aspiring to higher math. Students were quick to voice discontent. The material was simultaneously too easy and too hard, while connections to real-world issues were weak to non-existent. Recognizing the failure, UATX determined to improve. (Few universities acknowledge failure in their own programs, making improvement impossible.)

The *Quantitative Argumentation* approach, which greatly refined and coordinated many topics originally found in Macalester's QM4PP program, was the result. It helped that the primary faculty teaching the core course came from many directions of the quantitative world: David Ruth from naval leadership and nuclear engineering, Dorothy Dickmann from forensic accounting, and myself bringing in biology, economics, and epidemiology.

From 1900 on, universities have been organized around disciplines, groups of faculty with similar interests, backgrounds, and ambitions. Disciplines can become boosters of their individual perspectives and ignore others. 

A *team* provides a superior organization to “disciplines,” at least for education. Teams bring together different backgrounds and ambitions and build on their members' complementary strengths. Complementary weaknesses among the team faculty are also critical, since they bring pedagogical shortcomings to the fore and encourage compensatory revision. By embracing the failures of mainstream quantitative education, we can build an improved future.

- Daniel Kaplan, December 2026, Saint Paul, Minnesota
